To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the number of features per layer is a good indicator for a CNN's effective capacity, (2) the amount of learnable parameters in a CNN is not equally distributed across all layers, but is highest for intermediate layers, and (3) a network's effective capacity can be automatically increased in a bottom-up fashion by expanding layers with the least amount of features.
we introduce a novel bottom- up approach to expand representations and demonstrate that CNNs perform best when there is more capacity in intermediate layers, with falloff to earlier and later ones.

1) we propose a new method to automatically grow the width of individual layers in fixed-depth architectures, 2) this method can be used to determine feature importance and a network's effective capacity, 3) we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in improving performance and reducing the number of parameters in a variety of architectures, and 4) we observe that CNN architectures perform best with a non-monotonic increase in parameters, with more parameters in intermediate layers.

The main takeaway from our work is that

a network's effective capacity can be increased by expanding its representational capacity one feature at a times, and the amount of learnable parameters in a layer is not necessarily correlated with its importance.
a network architecture can be effectively expanded by greedily adding features to individual layers.
